summary: Gives guidelines for defining binary packet timestamp formats in network protocols at various layers, and recommends three timestamp formats. It helps protocol designers avoid common pitfalls. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Network messages often carry a clock reading. This document is advice for people designing new protocols on how to write that clock reading so everyone understands it and it stays useful.

what is the ntp 64-bit timestamp format

how to define a timestamp in a protocol
subtitle: A template for defining binary packet timestamps, plus three recommended formats from NTP and PTP.

tldr.problem: Many protocols carry a compact binary clock reading, but each one tends to define it differently and often leaves out details such as epoch, resolution, wraparound and leap seconds.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a template listing the attributes every timestamp specification must define, and recommends three ready-made formats: the NTP 64-bit, the NTP 32-bit and the PTP truncated format.
tldr.outcome: New protocols should normally reuse one of the three formats, which also lets them reuse existing hardware timestamping. If none fits, they follow the template.

facts.label: PTP truncated size
facts.value: 64 bits (low bits of the 80-bit PTP timestamp)

today: RFC 8877 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the RFC series' guide for defining binary packet timestamps.

sections.title: Why Packet Timestamps Need Guidelines
sections.content:
Timestamps are used in network protocols to log events, in delay measurement and clock synchronization protocols, and as part of nonces in security protocols. The RFC series uses two forms: text-based timestamps (RFC 3339), which are human-friendly strings, and packet timestamps, which are compact fixed-size binary fields not meant to be read by people.

This document covers only packet timestamps. It is a reference for protocol designers: consider the recommended formats first, and if none fits, define a new format using the template. A reused format also benefits from existing hardware timestamping, so a new protocol can be deployed quickly.
sections.eli5: Some clock readings are written for people, like 3:15 pm. Others are squeezed into a few bytes for computers. This document is about the squeezed kind.

sections.title: The Specification Template
sections.content:
A timestamp format specification MUST include at least the following aspects. For syntax, the size in bits or octets, with network order (big endian) assumed unless stated. For semantics:

  • Units and permitted ranges of each field.
  • Resolution, the smallest time unit used.
  • Wraparound, the period after which the value repeats.
  • Epoch, the origin of the timescale, such as UTC, or the moment a device was powered up.
  • Leap seconds, whether the timestamp is affected by them.

A synchronization aspects section is also expected, though it is not strictly part of the format. If a new format is needed, the specification should state why and derive it from an existing one where possible. The terminology also separates timestamp accuracy (mean of the error) from precision (variation of the error).
sections.eli5: When you write down a time, say how big the number is, what each part means, when counting started, and what happens when it runs out.

sections.title: The Three Recommended Formats
sections.content:
The NTP 64-bit format (from RFC 5905) has a 32-bit seconds field and a 32-bit fraction field, with a unit of 2^(-32) seconds, roughly 233 picoseconds. Its epoch is 1 January 1900 at 00:00 UTC, it is affected by leap seconds, and it wraps around every 2^(32) seconds, roughly 136 years, with the next wraparound in 2036.

The NTP 32-bit format uses 16 bits of seconds and 16 bits of fraction, with a unit of 2^(-16) seconds, roughly 15.3 microseconds. It has the same epoch and leap second behavior, and wraps around every 2^(16) seconds, roughly 18 hours. It suits cases where space is tight or the resolution and wraparound are enough.

The PTP truncated format is the 64 least significant bits of the 80-bit PTP timestamp: 32 bits of seconds and 32 bits of nanoseconds. The epoch is 1 January 1970 00:00:00 TAI, it is not affected by leap seconds, its resolution is 1 nanosecond, and it wraps every 2^(32) seconds, with the next wraparound in 2106.

Choice depends on size, resolution, wraparound period and whether protocols used together can share a format. NTP-based formats suit protocols that usually run with NTP, and PTP-based ones suit protocols on PTP-capable hardware.
sections.eli5: There are three ready-made clock formats. Two count from the year 1900 and one counts from 1970, and they differ in how finely they tick and how long until they run out.

sections.title: Synchronization and Leap Seconds
sections.content:
A protocol using a timestamp should include a Synchronization Aspects section. It says whether nodes must be synchronized with each other, whether time is measured against a central clock such as an NTP server, whether time follows a standard such as UTC or TAI, and what accuracy and precision are needed.

A leap second is a one-second adjustment occasionally applied to UTC to keep it aligned with solar time. A system clock may handle it in one of three ways: turn the clock back one second, freeze it during the leap second, or slow it down over a period called a leap smear that can range from several seconds to several hours. How leap seconds are handled depends on the synchronization protocol, so the RFC does not specify it.

Section 6 gives two hypothetical example specifications, one using the NTP 64-bit format and one using the PTP truncated format, and a table of protocols that use packet timestamps.
sections.eli5: Two clocks must agree for a timestamp to mean something. Sometimes the world adds one extra second to the day, and the protocol should say how it copes.

sections.title: Timestamp Control Fields
sections.content:
Some protocols want a control field that describes the structure and properties of a timestamp. Examples named are the Error Estimate field of RFC 4656 (used in OWAMP and TWAMP), the Root Dispersion and Root Delay fields in the NTP header, and the Correction Field in the PTP header.

The RFC lists high-level requirements for such fields: an extensible feature set, a good trade-off between features and size, a composition that says which elements are mandatory, conditional mandatory or optional, and a category split between static information (sent once per session) and runtime information (attached to each timestamp). Actual proposals are out of scope and will be defined in separate documents.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a timestamp comes with a note saying how sure the clock is. The RFC only sketches what such notes should look like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A protocol that uses a packet timestamp MUST specify the security considerations that result from it. Timestamps can aid network reconnaissance, since an eavesdropper can learn about performance and the level of synchronization between nodes. On-path attackers could spoof or modify timestamps, for example to skew delay measurements, and integrity protection such as Message Authentication Codes can mitigate this.

Delay attacks, where messages are maliciously delayed, cannot be prevented by cryptographic integrity protection. In some cases they can be mitigated by sending the information over multiple paths. Attacks on the underlying synchronization mechanism also affect timestamp users; attacks on time protocols are discussed in RFC 7384.
sections.eli5: Someone could peek at the clock readings or tamper with them, or hold messages back so they look slow. Locks help with tampering, but not with holding messages back.

fields.name: Fraction
fields.desc: Fractional seconds in units of 2^(-32) seconds.
